proposal.problem: The vehicle maintenance unit of the İstanbul provincial health directorate records every fault, maintenance visit and mileage reading of the ambulance fleet in the Portal's maintenance module (Bakım Onarım). The module stores what is typed but checks nothing against the other records of the same vehicle. A vehicle's current mileage, the mileage written on a fault record and the mileage history are three separate fields, and they drift apart. Between 1 September and 1 October 2026 the unit entered 1,702 fault records for 536 of the fleet's 577 active vehicles. In 49 of those records the mileage written on the fault is lower than the mileage of the same vehicle's previous fault, so the vehicle's mileage runs backwards; 45 vehicles are affected, about 8 percent of the vehicles that had a fault that month. Two more records jump by over 30,000 km between consecutive faults. None of this is flagged by the module. Today an error is found only when the unit notices a wrong maintenance due date or a fault that cannot be opened because the stored mileage is too high, and it is corrected by a developer reading the database by hand, about 5 hours a month; the rest stay in the records. On 17 October 2026 the module's own dashboard shows 45 vehicles past their periodic maintenance mileage and 17 approaching it, with no warning sent to anyone. Each uncorrected error delays or hides a periodic maintenance, which for an ambulance means a vehicle that may be off the road when it is needed.
proposal.mission: Give the Maintenance clerk and the Fleet supervisor of the vehicle maintenance unit a tool that reads the Portal's vehicle export, checks every maintenance, fault and mileage record against a written set of consistency rules, lists each violation with the rule it breaks, and warns which vehicles are approaching their periodic maintenance, so that record errors are found the week they are made rather than when a maintenance is missed, and nobody has to read the database by hand.
proposal.outcome: A maintenance clerk uploads the weekly export and within a minute sees which records contradict each other and why; the fleet supervisor opens the panel and sees which ambulances are due for periodic maintenance in the next two weeks, without asking a developer to query the database.

proposal.techWhy: RDFLib turns each export row into RDF statements about vehicles, readings, faults and visits, so the four Portal tables become one graph in which a vehicle's records can be compared. SHACL shapes, checked with pySHACL, state each consistency rule once, in a form the unit can read: a mileage reading may not be lower than the one before it, a repair may not be dated before its fault, a periodic maintenance mileage that is passed without a visit is a warning. A SKOS scheme holds the fault types, so 'motor' and 'MOTOR' are one concept. SPARQL queries over an Oxigraph store produce the report tables and the per-vehicle mileage rate used by the forecast. PROV-O records which export, which rule-set version and which run produced every report, so a correction can always be traced. The KVKK regime sets what the importer must strip before anything reaches the repository, and SHACL continuous-integration gates run the rules on every commit.

proposal.spec: The system reads the vehicle, maintenance, fault and mileage-history exports of the Portal as Excel or CSV files, replaces plates and names with codes, and builds an RDF graph of vehicles, mileage readings, fault records and maintenance visits, with fault types taken from a SKOS scheme. It validates the graph against a SHACL rule set in which each rule has a severity: mileage going backwards, a fault mileage above the vehicle's current mileage, a repair dated before its fault, a missing fault type and a periodic maintenance mileage that has been passed without a visit. It writes a report that names each violating record, the rule, the severity and the contradicting values, writes a correction-proposal file for the clerk, and records the run in PROV-O with the export's hash and the rule-set version. It computes each vehicle's average daily mileage from the history and forecasts the date its periodic maintenance falls due. A web panel shows violations per vehicle, the monthly trend and the vehicles due within a chosen number of days. When an export is missing a table or a required column, the tool stops and names the missing part instead of checking a partial graph.

scenarios.text: Given an export in which vehicle A017 has a mileage reading of 84,300 followed by a fault recorded at 83,900, when the clerk runs the check, then the report lists the fault record under the rule 'mileage may not go backwards' with both values
Given an export in which the mileage-history table is missing, when the clerk runs the check, then the tool produces no report and says which table is missing
Given a vehicle whose periodic maintenance mileage equals its current mileage exactly, when the check runs, then the vehicle appears as due today and not as overdue
Given a vehicle with no mileage reading at all, when the check runs, then the forecast for that vehicle says 'no history' instead of a date

proposal.activity: The clerk exports the four tables from the Portal and uploads them. The importer checks that every table and required column is present; if one is missing it stops and names it. Otherwise it anonymises plates and names, builds the graph and loads it into the store. The validator runs the SHACL rules; each violation is collected with its severity. The reporter writes the HTML and CSV report and the correction proposal, and records the run in PROV-O. The forecaster computes each vehicle's daily mileage rate and its due date. The panel reads the latest run and shows the summary; the clerk corrects the named records in the Portal and the next weekly run shows whether the violations are gone.
proposal.sequence: The clerk sends the export files to the command-line tool. The tool asks the importer to parse and anonymise them and receives a graph. It sends the graph to the Oxigraph store, then asks pySHACL to validate the graph against the rule set and receives a validation report. It passes the report to the reporter, which queries the store with SPARQL for the contradicting values and writes the files. The reporter asks the provenance recorder to store the run. The panel, when opened by the supervisor, queries the store for the latest run, the per-vehicle counts and the forecast, and renders the page.

proposal.classModel: Vehicle has a code, a current mileage, a periodic maintenance mileage and many MileageReadings, FaultRecords and MaintenanceVisits. MileageReading has a date and a value. FaultRecord has a date, a mileage and a FaultType from the SKOS scheme. MaintenanceVisit has a date, a mileage, a kind (periodic or corrective) and an optional repaired FaultRecord. Rule has an identifier, a text, a severity and a SHACL shape. Violation links one record to one Rule with the contradicting values. CheckRun has a date, the export hash, the rule-set version and many Violations; it is a PROV-O activity that used the export and generated the report. Forecast belongs to a Vehicle and has a daily rate and a due date.

proposal.model_Data: Design-level class diagram: Vehicle, MileageReading, FaultRecord, MaintenanceVisit, FaultType, Rule, Violation, CheckRun and Forecast as in the class model. VehicleShape requires a code and a periodic maintenance mileage; ReadingShape requires a date and a non-negative value; FaultShape requires a FaultType from the scheme; VisitShape requires a date not earlier than its repaired fault; CheckRun is a prov:Activity that used the export entity and generated the report entity.
proposal.model_Architecture: Component diagram: Importer (openpyxl, pandas) feeds Anonymiser (regex) feeds GraphBuilder (RDFLib); Store (Oxigraph) holds the graph; Validator (pySHACL) reads the rule set and the graph and emits violations; Reporter (Jinja2 templates, csv) and ProvenanceRecorder (RDFLib, PROV-O) write the outputs; Forecaster reads the store over SPARQL; Panel (FastAPI) reads the store and the latest run. The command-line entry point orders them; the Portal is outside the system and only its export files cross the boundary.
proposal.model_Interface: Component diagram of the boundaries: the command-line tool takes a folder with the four export files (vehicles, readings, faults, visits as .xlsx or .csv with named columns) and writes report.html, report.csv, corrections.csv and run.ttl into a dated folder; the panel exposes GET / for the summary, GET /vehicle/{code} for one vehicle's violations and forecast, and GET /runs/{id} for a run's provenance as JSON-LD. Nothing is written to the Portal.
proposal.model_User_interface: Panel: a header with the date of the latest run and the violation count; a table of vehicles with code, violations, forecast due date and a 'due within 14 days' mark, sortable by each column; a monthly trend chart below; clicking a vehicle opens its violations with the rule text and the contradicting values. One page, readable on an office desktop browser without training.
proposal.libraries: openpyxl and pandas read the Excel and CSV exports; regular expressions anonymise plates and names and scan the outputs; dataclasses and typing describe vehicles, readings, faults and visits; generators stream rows into the graph; a decorator times and logs each stage; a context manager opens and closes the Oxigraph store; concurrent.futures loads the four tables in parallel; argparse builds the command-line tool; logging writes the run log; pytest and GitHub Actions test every rule; RDFLib, pySHACL and Jinja2 build, validate and report the graph; FastAPI serves the panel. Course topics applied: object-oriented design, iterators and generators, decorators and context managers, regular expressions, concurrency, testing, packaging with pyproject and a command-line interface.
